title: Chapter 17. Of the Causes, Generation, and Definition of a Commonwealth
paragraphs: The final cause, end, or design of men (who naturally love liberty and dominion over others) in laying upon themselves the restraint in which we see them live in commonwealths is the foresight of their own preservation, and of a more contented life thereby — that is, of getting themselves out of the miserable condition of war which is the necessary consequence (as has been shown) of the natural passions of men when there is no visible power to keep them in awe, and to bind them, by fear of punishment, to the performance of their covenants and the observance of those laws of nature set down in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters.

For the laws of nature — justice, equity, modesty, mercy, and (in short) doing to others as we would be done by — are by themselves, without the terror of some power to enforce them, contrary to our natural passions, which carry us to partiality, pride, revenge, and the like. And covenants without the sword are only words, with no strength to secure a man at all. So, in spite of the laws of nature (which each man keeps when he has the will to keep them and can do so safely), if there is no power erected, or none great enough for our security, every man will and may lawfully rely on his own strength and skill as his guard against all other men. In all places where men have lived in small families, robbing and despoiling one another has been a trade, and so far from being reckoned as contrary to the law of nature, the greater the spoils gained, the greater the honour. The only laws they observed in this were the laws of honour: to abstain from cruelty, to leave men their lives and the instruments of farming. And as small families did then, so cities and kingdoms — which are only larger families — do now. For their own security they enlarge their dominions, using as pretexts every danger and every fear of invasion, or of aid that might be given to invaders, and try as far as they can to subdue or weaken their neighbours, by open force and by secret arts, for want of any other guarantee — and they consider this just, and are remembered for it in later ages with honour.

Nor is it the mere joining together of a small number of men that gives them this security. In small numbers, a small addition on one side or the other makes such a great difference in strength that it is enough to decide the victory, and so gives encouragement to an invasion. The multitude sufficient to rely on for our security is not fixed at any specific number, but is decided by comparison with the enemy we fear; and it is sufficient when the enemy's advantage is not so visibly and conspicuously decisive of the outcome of a war as to move him to attempt one.

And let the multitude be ever so great: if their actions are directed by their individual judgements and individual appetites, they can expect from that no defence nor protection — neither against a common enemy nor against the injuries of one another. For being divided in opinion about the best use of their strength, they do not help but hinder each other, and reduce their strength by mutual opposition to nothing. By this they are easily not only subdued by a very few who agree together, but, when there is no common enemy, they make war on each other for their particular interests. For if we could suppose a great multitude of men to agree in observing justice and the other laws of nature without a common power to keep them all in awe, we might as well suppose all mankind to do the same; and then there neither would be, nor would there need to be, any civil government or commonwealth at all, because there would be peace without subjection.

Nor is it enough, for the security that men want to last all their life long, to be governed and directed by one judgement for a limited time — as in one battle, or one war. For though they win a victory by their united effort against a foreign enemy, yet afterwards, when either they have no common enemy, or the one that one side counts as an enemy is counted as a friend by another, they must inevitably, through their different interests, dissolve and fall back into war among themselves.

It is true that certain living creatures — bees and ants — live sociably with one another (which is why Aristotle numbers them among the political creatures); and yet they have no other direction than their individual judgements and appetites, nor any speech by which one of them can communicate to another what it thinks expedient for the common benefit. So one might want to know why mankind cannot do the same. To this I answer:

First, that men are continually in competition for honour and dignity, which these creatures are not; and so among men there arises on that ground envy and hatred, and finally war — but among these creatures, no such thing.

Second, that among these creatures the common good does not differ from the private good; and being inclined by nature to their private good, they thereby procure the common benefit. But man, whose joy consists in comparing himself with other men, can relish nothing that is not eminent.

Third, that these creatures, not having (as man does) the use of reason, do not see, or think they see, any fault in the administration of their common business. Whereas among men there are many who think themselves wiser, and better able to govern the public, than the rest; and these strive to reform and innovate, one in this direction, another in that, and thereby bring it into discord and civil war.

Fourth, that these creatures, though they have some use of voice in making known to one another their desires and other affections, lack the art of words, by which some men can represent to others good in the likeness of evil, and evil in the likeness of good, and magnify or diminish the apparent size of good and evil — making men discontented and disturbing their peace at will.

Fifth, irrational creatures cannot distinguish between injury and damage; and so, so long as they are at ease, they are not offended with their fellows. Man, on the other hand, is most troublesome when he is most at ease: for then is when he loves to show off his wisdom and to find fault with the actions of those who govern the commonwealth.

Last, the agreement of these creatures is natural; that of men is by covenant only, which is artificial. So it is no wonder that something more (besides covenant) is needed to make their agreement constant and lasting — namely, a common power, to keep them in awe and to direct their actions to the common benefit.

The only way to erect such a common power as may be able to defend them from the invasion of foreigners and from the injuries done by one to another — and so to secure them in such a way that by their own industry and by the fruits of the earth they may feed themselves and live contentedly — is to transfer all their power and strength upon one man, or upon one assembly of men, that may reduce all their wills, by plurality of votes, to one will. This is the same as appointing one man, or one assembly of men, to bear their person; and every one to own and acknowledge himself the author of whatever the bearer of their person shall do, or cause to be done, in those things that concern the common peace and safety — and to that end to submit each one's will to his will, and each one's judgement to his judgement. This is more than consent, or concord: it is a real unity of them all in one and the same person, made by covenant of every man with every man, in such a way that it is as if every man should say to every man, 'I authorise, and give up, my right of governing myself, to this man, or to this assembly of men, on this condition: that you give up your right to him, and authorise all his actions in like manner.' This done, the multitude so united in one person is called a COMMONWEALTH — in Latin, CIVITAS. This is the generation of that great LEVIATHAN, or rather (to speak more reverently) of that mortal god, to which, under the immortal God, we owe our peace and defence. For by this authority, given to him by every particular man in the commonwealth, he has the use of so much power and strength conferred on him that, by the terror of it, he is enabled to mould the wills of them all to peace at home and to mutual aid against their enemies abroad.

And in him consists the essence of the commonwealth — which (to define it) is: one person, of whose acts a great multitude, by mutual covenants one with another, have made themselves every one the author, to the end that he may use the strength and means of them all as he shall think expedient for their peace and common defence.
And the one who bears this person is called the SOVEREIGN, and is said to have sovereign power; and every other man is his SUBJECT.

There are two ways of attaining this sovereign power. One is by natural force — as when a man compels his children to submit themselves and their children to his government, being able to destroy them if they refuse; or when by war he subdues his enemies to his will, sparing their lives on that condition. The other is when men agree among themselves to submit voluntarily to some man, or some assembly of men, trusting that they will be protected by him against all others. The latter may be called a political commonwealth, or commonwealth by institution; the former, a commonwealth by acquisition. I shall speak first of the commonwealth by institution.
